summary: Earth Trend Detective is a free web tool that lets anyone investigate how Earth is changing. You spin a 3D globe, click any place, choose variables such as temperature, rain, snow or soil moisture, and set the years. The tool charts 45 years of NASA data for that place and tests whether each trend is statistically significant, then explains the result in plain language. It answers the challenge's four questions directly: what is changing, where, by how much, and whether the change is significant. It matters because it turns NASA's open Earth data into evidence that students and the public can test themselves, and it shows that the same climate process can push a variable up in one region and down in another.
details: What it does: Earth Trend Detective guides the user through a real trend analysis in three steps. (1) Where: spin the interactive 3D globe and click any point on Earth, or search one of 38 ready places covering every climate type: the Arctic and Antarctic, deserts, rainforests, megacities, deltas, farmland, mountains and open ocean. Clicking any other point fetches that exact location live from the NASA POWER API. (2) What: pick one or more of 13 variables shown as simple icon tiles with plain-language definitions: air temperature, heat extremes, rain, snow depth, soil moisture, sunlight, night-time lows, surface temperature, evaporation, humidity, water vapour, cloud cover and wind. (3) When: drag a year slider to choose any period from 1981 to 2025. Results: for each variable the tool shows the rate of change per decade as a large clear number, a time-series chart with the trend line and its 95% confidence band, a "warming stripes" bar with one stripe per year, and a plain-language verdict (significant trend, tests disagree, weak hint, or not significant). A "Where is it changing?" chart and the colour of every dot on the globe compare the same variable at all 38 places, so users can see trends running in opposite directions. When a trend is not yet significant, the tool estimates how many more years of data would be needed. How it works: the seasonal cycle is removed by subtracting each calendar month's long-term mean (anomalies); users can also analyse yearly means or a single month. The trend is fitted by least squares and tested with a two-sided t-test whose sample size is reduced for month-to-month autocorrelation. A seasonal Mann-Kendall test with the Hirsch-Slack correction gives a second, non-parametric opinion, and Sen's slope gives a robust rate. The globe is coloured with a global 2 m air temperature climatology from NASA POWER. All statistics are written from scratch in JavaScript and were checked against an independent Python calculation. Learning features: three guided demo cases (Arctic warming; rainfall rising in the Sahel while falling in the Amazon; El Nino hiding a trend) walk new users through the method step by step. A field guide explains every variable. Benefits and impact: no installation, account or coding needed; works on phones; open source. It teaches the full scientific workflow: choose a variable and region, visualise the time series, measure the rate of change and test its significance. We want students and the public to become data detectives who check climate claims against NASA data for their own region. Next steps: more NASA datasets (GPM IMERG rainfall, MODIS vegetation, GLDAS soil moisture), regional trend maps, and an Arabic interface. Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript; three.js for the 3D globe; topojson-client for coastlines; Python for downloading and packaging the NASA data; GitHub Pages for hosting. Source code: https://github.com/faris-mo/earth-trend-detective
